```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5)
```


A selected model still has to be checked. This vignette covers the
diagnostic functions of arimatools, the deterministic terms of integrated
models, recursive parameter stability, and intervention (outlier) models:
regressors for dates you choose, automatic detection, and effect plots.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(forecast)
library(arimatools)
```

## The diagnostic battery

We use one realization of the ARMA(1,1)
$Y_t = 0.7Y_{t-1} + u_t + 0.4u_{t-1}$ and a misspecified AR(1).

```{r}
set.seed(12345)
y <- arima.sim(model = list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.4), n = 300, n.start = 200)
fit_ar1    <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 0), include.mean = FALSE)
fit_arma11 <- Arima(y, order = c(1, 0, 1), include.mean = FALSE)
```

No single diagnostic answers every question. The table below maps each
question to a function.

| Question | Function |
|---|---|
| Are the coefficients precisely estimated? | `coefficient_diagnostics()` |
| Are the residuals serially uncorrelated? | `plot_residual_diagnostics()`, `ljung_box_test()`, `residual_correlations()` |
| Are the residuals approximately normal? | `jarque_bera_test()` |
| Is the AR part causal and the MA part invertible? | `root_summary()`, `root_diagnostics()`, `is_causal()`, `is_invertible()` |
| Are there (near-)common AR and MA roots? | `common_roots()`, `plot_inverse_roots()` |
| Are the parameter estimates highly correlated? | `parameter_correlation()` |
| Are the parameters stable through the sample? | `recursive_estimation()`, `plot_parameter_stability()` |

### Residual correlation

`plot_residual_diagnostics()` stacks the residuals, their ACF and PACF with
white-noise bounds, and the Ljung-Box p-values by lag with a 5% reference
line.

```{r, fig.height = 9}
plot_residual_diagnostics(fit_arma11, lags = 20,
                          title = "Residual Diagnostics: ARMA(1,1)")
```

`ljung_box_test()` gives the statistics at chosen lags. Degrees of freedom
are corrected for the estimated ARMA coefficients, $h - (p + q)$, so only
lags larger than $p + q$ are accepted.

```{r, error = TRUE}
ljung_box_test(fit_arma11, lags = c(8, 12, 20))
ljung_box_test(fit_ar1, lags = c(8, 12, 20))
ljung_box_test(fit_arma11, lags = 2)
```

The Ljung-Box test is a portmanteau test with low power against particular
alternatives: a non-rejection is not proof of white noise. Look at the
whole sequence of p-values and at the correlograms.

### Normality

```{r}
jarque_bera_test(fit_arma11)
```

### Roots, cancellation and parameter correlation

```{r}
root_summary(fit_arma11)
root_diagnostics(fit_arma11)
parameter_correlation(fit_arma11)
```

An overparameterized model shows the problem directly. Fitted to the same
ARMA(1,1) data, an ARMA(4,4) has AR and MA inverse roots that nearly cancel
in pairs (distance below `tol = 0.05`). They are marked with a cross in the
inverse-root plot.

```{r, fig.height = 5}
fit_arma44 <- Arima(y, order = c(4, 0, 4), include.mean = FALSE,
                    optim.control = list(maxit = 1000))
common_roots(fit_arma44)
plot_inverse_roots(fit_arma44, title = "Inverse Roots: ARMA(4,4)")
```

The model-building vignette shows how these pairs mislead the top-lag test
in a General-to-Specific reduction.

## Integration and deterministic terms

The meaning of a constant depends on where differencing enters. With $d=1$,
$\Delta y_t = c + \varepsilon_t$ implies a linear trend in the level:
`forecast::Arima()` calls this constant *drift* and estimates it with
`include.drift = TRUE`. With $d = 2$, `forecast::Arima()` does not allow a
constant at all.

When $d$ is not fixed, `auto_arima()` chooses it before the ARMA search, by
repeated KPSS tests (`forecast::ndiffs()`); information criteria are then
used only among models with that $d$.

```{r}
set.seed(202609)
y_i1 <- ts(cumsum(0.08 + rnorm(250)))
auto_i1 <- auto_arima(y_i1, criterion = "BIC", max_p = 4, max_q = 4)
auto_arima_summary(auto_i1)
```

`auto_arima_summary()` spells out the deterministic component: a mean for
$d = 0$, a drift (a linear trend in the level) for $d = 1$. The order of
integration is itself an estimate: `ndiffs(y, test = "adf")` or
`test = "pp"` can disagree with the default KPSS choice.

## Parameter stability

An ARIMA specification assumes constant parameters. We simulate an AR(1)
whose coefficient changes from 0.35 to 0.85 halfway through the sample.

```{r}
set.seed(901)
n <- 320; tb <- 160
e <- rnorm(n); y_break <- numeric(n)
for (t in 2:n) y_break[t] <- (if (t <= tb) 0.35 else 0.85) * y_break[t - 1] + e[t]
```

`recursive_estimation()` re-estimates the model on expanding windows
$1{:}m, 1{:}(m+1), \dots, 1{:}n$ and returns a long table with estimates,
standard errors and confidence intervals for each coefficient (and the
innovation variance) at every endpoint.

```{r}
rec <- recursive_estimation(y_break, order = c(1, 0, 0), initial = 80,
                            include.constant = FALSE)
head(rec)
```

`plot_parameter_stability()` plots the recursive estimates with their
confidence bands, the full-sample estimate as a dashed line, and an
optional vertical reference line at a known or hypothesized break.

```{r}
plot_parameter_stability(rec, breakpoint = tb)
```

The break line is a visual reference, not a test. For formal stability tests
and break dating (CUSUM, sup-F, Bai-Perron) on the AR regression, see the
'strucchange' package.

## Interventions: regression with ARIMA errors

With `xreg`, `forecast::Arima()` estimates a regression with ARIMA errors,

$$
y_t = X_t\beta + u_t, \qquad \Phi(L)(1 - L)^d u_t = \Theta(L)\varepsilon_t .
$$

The differencing belongs to the error process. A pulse in $X_t$ is therefore
a one-period additive outlier in the observed $y_t$ for every $d$. It is not
an innovation pulse in the differenced equation, which would become a step
($d = 1$) or a ramp ($d = 2$) in the level. The regressor must match the
intervention you mean.

`outlier_regressors()` builds the three standard intervention regressors
for an outlier at observation $t_0$:

| Type | Regressor | Effect on the observed series |
|---|---|---|
| `"AO"`, additive outlier | 1 at $t_0$, 0 elsewhere | one-period pulse |
| `"LS"`, level shift | 1 from $t_0$ onwards | permanent step |
| `"TC"`, temporary change | $\delta^{t - t_0}$ from $t_0$ onwards | pulse decaying at rate $\delta$ |

Dates are checked against the frequency of the series; columns are named by
type and period.

```{r}
yq <- ts(rnorm(100), start = c(2000, 1), frequency = 4)   # 2000Q1-2024Q4
X <- outlier_regressors(yq, dates = c("2008Q4", "2020Q2", "2020Q3"),
                        types = c("LS", "AO", "TC"), delta = 0.7)
colnames(X)
attr(X, "outliers")
```

Series without calendar time use `positions` (observation numbers) instead
of `dates`.

### An additive outlier

We contaminate one observation of an AR(1) with an additive outlier of size
$\omega = 8$ and estimate the intervention jointly with the error model.

```{r}
set.seed(440)
n_ao <- 260; t0 <- 151
u <- as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.65), n = n_ao))
y_ao <- u; y_ao[t0] <- y_ao[t0] + 8

X_ao <- outlier_regressors(y_ao, positions = t0, types = "AO")
fit_ao <- Arima(y_ao, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = X_ao, include.mean = FALSE)
coefficient_diagnostics(fit_ao)
```

The observation is neither deleted nor replaced: its exceptional effect is
estimated, with a standard error. Compare the AR coefficient when the
outlier is ignored:

```{r}
coef(Arima(y_ao, order = c(1, 0, 0), include.mean = FALSE))["ar1"]
```

`plot_outliers()` accepts any model whose regressors were built by
`outlier_regressors()`. It shows the observed and outlier-adjusted series,
with outlier dates marked by type, and the combined outlier effect.

```{r, fig.height = 6}
plot_outliers(fit_ao, title = "Additive outlier: estimated effect")
```

### Several interventions: specification and effects

With several interventions it helps to look at the specification before
estimating it. `plot_interventions()` without a model shows the series with
the chosen dates, marked by type. Below, a quarterly AR(1) receives an
additive outlier in 2004Q4, a temporary change in 2008Q4 and a level shift in
2012Q2.

```{r}
set.seed(321)
yq <- ts(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.6), n = 120), start = c(1990, 1), frequency = 4)
Xq <- outlier_regressors(yq, dates = c("2004Q4", "2008Q4", "2012Q2"),
                         types = c("AO", "TC", "LS"), delta = 0.7)
yq <- yq + as.numeric(unclass(Xq) %*% c(5, -4, 3))   # true effects 5, -4, 3
plot_interventions(yq, Xq)
```

After estimation, `intervention_effects()` gives each estimated
contribution (coefficient times regressor), their sum and the adjusted
series, and `plot_interventions()` with the model draws them.

```{r, fig.height = 6}
fit_q <- Arima(yq, order = c(1, 0, 0), xreg = Xq)
eff <- intervention_effects(fit_q, Xq)
round(attr(eff, "coefficients"), 2)
eff[c(59:61, 76:79), ]
plot_interventions(yq, Xq, fit_q, individual = TRUE)
```

The adjusted series is not a residual: the AR dynamics and the mean are
still in it. It is the series with the estimated intervention effects
removed.

### Automatic detection

`detect_outliers()` applies the iterative procedure of Chen and Liu (1993),
as implemented in `tsoutliers::tso()`, to a nonseasonal ARIMA model, and
re-estimates the final model with regressors from `outlier_regressors()`.
The model can be given as a fitted model, as a fixed order, or left to
AutoARIMA. It requires the 'tsoutliers' package.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("tsoutliers", quietly = TRUE)}
found <- detect_outliers(y_ao, order = c(1, 0, 0), include.constant = FALSE)
found
```

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("tsoutliers", quietly = TRUE), fig.height = 6}
plot_outliers(found, title = "Detected outlier effects")
```

The result also contains the final model (`found$fit`), the regressors, the
combined effect and the adjusted series. Supported models are univariate
and nonseasonal, with an optional mean or drift; models with other
regressors or a Box-Cox transformation are rejected.

A detected outlier is a candidate, not an explanation. The reported standard
errors treat the selected dates and types as known and ignore the search
that found them. With many candidate dates, some observations will be
flagged by chance. Detection finds candidates to be judged with economic
knowledge.

### Interactive figures

Every plotting function accepts `interactive = TRUE` and then returns a
'plotly' widget with tooltips, e.g.
`plot_outliers(fit_ao, interactive = TRUE)`.

Forecasting from these models is covered in
`vignette("forecasting", package = "arimatools")`.
